overview: The atlas calls this layer “Plateau fichers and hunter gatherers.” “Fichers” is a spelling mistake preserved in the exact database name; “fishers” was almost certainly intended. The color is also an editorial umbrella, not one ancient people. Its changing polygon sweeps across parts of interior British Columbia, Washington, Oregon, Idaho and Montana, where distinct communities spoke different languages. Archaeology reveals winter pithouse villages, seasonal camps, salmon fisheries, deer hunting, root grounds, berry patches, stone and bone tools, exchange and food storage. Yet no single recipe fits every river, upland or century. Regional food records refuse one simple salmon-only story for every interior valley. At Bridge River, floors and cache pits reveal changing households. Camas bulbs preserve expert land care without becoming a domesticated crop. The map vanishes in 1492, returns with a hole in 1500, shrinks dramatically in 1530 and ends in 1600. Those are atlas seams, not disappearances. Nimiipuu, Yakama, Spokane, Schitsu'umsh, Ktunaxa, St'at'imc, Syilx and many other living nations continue. Their histories must remain distinct, even while this card explores shared questions about life across the broad interior.

periods.title: 1500 to 1000 BCE: one giant map color, many local histories
periods.summary: The first target polygon already covers an implausibly vast interior, from central British Columbia toward Oregon, Idaho and western Montana. Archaeologists instead build local sequences from dated houses, camps, fish bones, roots and tools. The atlas boundary is a viewing device, not evidence for one founding population.

periods.title: 1000 to 500 BCE: houses and seasonal rounds vary by valley
periods.summary: Regional evidence includes winter pithouses and repeated seasonal camps, but their timing differs between the Fraser, Columbia, Snake and upland basins. People scheduled fishing, hunting, gathering and storage around local abundance. A house form or projectile point cannot by itself define a tribe or language.

periods.title: 500 BCE to 1 BCE: food security is built from diversity
periods.summary: Fish, deer, elk, roots, berries and other foods entered different local combinations. Storage and hot-rock cooking supported winter life, while small point styles help researchers discuss changing weapons only when securely dated. Tiny atlas coordinate changes in 100 and 1 BCE do not mark cultural revolutions.

periods.title: 1 to 500 CE: rivers connect places without making them identical
periods.summary: Salmon moved through major river systems, while people, tools and information crossed uplands and tributaries. Ancient fish DNA can identify species that ordinary bone shape may miss. The broad polygon stays stable in sampled membership, but archaeological communities remained locally organized and culturally diverse.

periods.title: 500 to 800 CE: villages, stores and household choices
periods.summary: At Middle Fraser sites, houses, storage and salmon supported substantial winter communities, yet families differed in work and access to food. Bridge River records many rebuilding floors rather than one frozen village plan. In 800 the atlas clips its northwest edge, a cartographic adjustment rather than a dated migration.

periods.title: 800 to 1000 CE: climate questions need several kinds of evidence
periods.summary: Kettle Falls dates and Middle Fraser studies test whether changing salmon runs, climate and settlement rhythms affected activity. No single cause explains every abandoned or rebuilt house. The 1000 atlas geometry changes by tiny coordinate amounts while tested target membership remains the same.

periods.title: 1000 to 1279 CE: large houses do not equal one government
periods.summary: Bridge River Housepit 54 held several families and changed across successive floors. Storage, hearths and sleeping or work areas reveal household organization, while evidence for inequality appeared in particular phases. Researchers debate cooperation, autonomy and leadership without turning every Plateau village into a centralized state.

periods.title: 1279 to 1492 CE: networks and local authority endure
periods.summary: The 1279 and 1400 maps have separate coordinate signatures, but that precision belongs to the modern basemap. Communities maintained fisheries, root grounds, exchange and political relationships at their own scales. Rock art and unusual structures add evidence for gathering and ceremony without revealing one umbrella-wide religion.

periods.title: 1492 to 1530 CE: an atlas gap, return and sudden split
periods.summary: The exact target is absent in 1492 while numerous named Indigenous layers occupy sampled places. It returns in 1500 with a hole around sampled Nimiipuu-area points, then becomes two small remnants in 1530. These seams expose editorial redrawing; they cannot date cultural disappearance, migration or replacement.

periods.title: 1530 to 1600 CE: the umbrella ends while peoples continue
periods.summary: Only a tiny central Washington sliver and a northern component remain in 1530. At 1600 the broad target disappears among distinct named layers. This is not a fall. Living Plateau nations preserve their own governments, languages, teachings and responsibilities, and later colonial change must be narrated through those specific histories.

sections.title: Read the typo, polygon and evidence before reading a culture

items.text: The exact atlas id and display name say “fichers,” apparently a misspelling of “fishers.” The card keeps that database identity so links work, then explains the error. No known people called themselves this phrase. It is a modern map category and must never replace a community's own name.

At 1500 BCE the single polygon includes sampled Kamloops, Prince George, Spokane, Boise, Burns, Missoula and Kalispell, yet excludes Seattle, Celilo Falls, Bend and Klamath Falls. That strange footprint is too broad and jagged to be a surveyed cultural border. The geometry audit, not the word “Plateau,” controls this card's scope.

Archaeologists distinguish direct finds from interpretation. A charred bulb is direct plant evidence; radiocarbon helps date its context; experiments suggest how an earth oven worked; a later community account may explain a comparable practice. None of those lines automatically proves what every household believed or called the food.

Contemporaneous written-language sample: none represents this exact atlas umbrella. Original script: unavailable. Transliteration: unavailable. Translation: unavailable. Peoples here certainly had languages and rich oral knowledge. Modern Nimipuutimt and Snchitsu'umshtsn writing systems are valuable living achievements, but borrowing either would falsely make one language speak for many and for earlier centuries.

Ancient DNA can identify a salmon species or explore human ancestry, but it cannot name a person's language, nation, bedtime story or political allegiance. Even a large fish-bone dataset represents excavated places and preservation conditions. Strong research combines molecules, context, tools, houses, landscapes and Indigenous knowledge without flattening their different questions.

sections.title: Move through rivers, grasslands, forests and seasonal weather

items.text: The mapped interior crosses dry plateaus, mountain passes, forests, lakes and huge river basins. Snow, spring floods, salmon timing, root growth and berry ripening created different calendars. The Williams Lake assessment records winter villages and shorter-use sites, showing that “mobile” and “settled” were seasonal choices rather than opposite kinds of people.

Upper Lillooet, Middle Fraser and nearby communities gathered in winter settlements and traveled to fisheries, hunting areas and plant grounds. The Lillooet assessment keeps St'at'imc, Nlaka'pamux and Secwepemc histories locally distinguished. Similar pithouses do not erase political borders, dialects, marriage ties or different routes.

Purposeful low-intensity fire could maintain open camas habitat and influence future harvests, but burn timing, frequency and place mattered. Lightning also burned the Plateau. Researchers therefore avoid imagining one uniform “fire regime.” Skilled stewardship means reading wind, fuel, plants and responsibility, not simply setting the landscape ablaze.

Pend Oreille camas bulbs show people repeatedly selected mature plants while leaving smaller bulbs to grow. This is land management and careful harvesting, not proof that camas became a domesticated crop. Mobility could shift between pithouse winters and lighter warm-season shelters while people returned to productive grounds over generations.

Camas restoration at Weippe Prairie links archaeology, ecology and Nimiipuu priorities. Modern farming, invasive plants and changed disturbance patterns damaged a cultural landscape, while collaborative work supports its renewal. Continuity here is active stewardship in the present, not a claim that every ancient harvesting technique remained unchanged.

sections.title: Combine salmon, game, roots and berries into local food systems

items.text: Salmon were crucial at many Columbia and Fraser fisheries, but “salmon people” cannot explain every meal. Ancient Chinook bones reveal several lineages and changing abundance, while upland sites may emphasize deer or plants. Fish also carried oil, labor schedules, ceremony and exchange, so counting bones is only one part of food history.

A Late Archaic pithouse at Pine Creek in the John Day uplands contained abundant deer evidence rather than the salmon-heavy pattern expected beside major rivers. That local counterexample matters. The broad atlas color includes river, foothill and basin economies; it cannot turn them all into copies of Celilo or Kettle Falls.

Roots such as camas could become sweet and digestible after long, controlled cooking. Earth ovens used heated stone, plant packing and patient timing. Experimental and later Kalispel comparisons illuminate that process without proving one ancient recipe. Fun fact: a proper camas bake could outlast a modern movie marathon by a very wide margin.

A later visitor story says people unfamiliar with camas ate far too much and suffered memorable stomach trouble. Nimiipuu experts understood harvesting and preparation; the joke belongs on the overeager guests, not the food. The account is historical comparison, while ancient bulbs and ovens provide the earlier direct evidence.

The CTUIR First Foods framework begins with water and follows salmon, deer, roots and berries through seasons and reciprocal responsibilities. It is a living tribal teaching, not a generic prehistoric menu. Used carefully, it helps children see food as relationships among places, ceremonies, work and care rather than grocery items.

sections.title: Process, store, craft and exchange without a single technology timeline

items.text: Pithouse villages often contain hearths, roasting features and storage pits, but pits could change purpose or be emptied before abandonment. In the Arrow region, archaeologists connect features with salmon fishing, root cooking and seasonal settlement only through their contents and context. A hole in the floor is evidence to test, not a ready-made label.

Housepit 54 at Bridge River preserves seventeen floors, cache pits, a cooking or roasting area, refuse zones and a flint knapper's toolkit. Rebuilding makes one house a long sequence of decisions. Researchers working with Xwisten can ask how household space changed instead of treating the final floor as the whole story.

At Keatley Creek, ancient DNA helped identify salmon in a storage-pit deposit where articulated vertebrae suggested fish entered together. Storage reduced winter risk, but preservation and sampling shape what survives. One pit cannot reveal every family's yearly supply, ownership rule or success in a bad run.

Stone came from sources that could lie far from a village, while baskets, foods and information moved through networks that leave uneven traces. Trade did not require a capital or merchant class. Gifts, visits, marriage, shared fisheries and specialist skill could connect autonomous households and communities in several overlapping ways.

Fishing platforms, dip nets and hoop nets required wood, fiber or twine, pitch, river knowledge and coordinated labor. The Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission describes these as living tribal technologies. Archaeology may preserve stone weights or posts better than nets, so absence of fiber is not absence of engineering.

sections.title: Build homes, clothing and tidy camps with perishable materials

items.text: Winter pithouses used an excavated floor, posts, roof materials, a central hearth and planned storage or work areas, but size and arrangement varied. A roof could also serve as an entrance in some reconstructions. That makes a cozy kid image: visiting might begin by walking over the house before climbing inside.

Warm-season shelters could use poles, tule or other mats, bark and hide, leaving much fainter traces than deep winter houses. Culturally modified trees along the Nez Perce Trail preserve bark or cambium harvesting. Those marks show skilled plant use, while later shelter descriptions remain localized Nimiipuu comparison.

Trees and shrubs supplied wood for tools and frames, bark and fiber for cordage, containers and coverings, plus medicines and foods. The National Park Service account is specific to Nez Perce country and historical knowledge. It helps explain missing perishable objects without turning one nation's plant vocabulary into a Plateau-wide catalog.

No reviewed source documents one umbrella-wide toilet, latrine, sewer or sanitation code. Camps and houses instead preserve hearth ash, food refuse, broken tools and outdoor discard areas. People could move waste away from sleeping and cooking spaces, but archaeology rarely lets us point to a pit and confidently announce, “bathroom.”

Water safety depended on springs, streams, lakes and rivers, plus local knowledge of season and contamination. The CTUIR Upland Vision places water before other First Foods because fish, game, roots, berries and people depend on it. That is a present tribal framework with deep responsibility, not proof of one ancient plumbing system.

sections.title: Keep family, women, kin and leadership locally grounded

items.text: A large pithouse could hold several related families, but floor area produces an estimate rather than a census. At Bridge River, household size, storage and wealth signals changed over time. Co-residence does not reveal every marriage, adoption or caregiving bond, and one unusually large house cannot define all Plateau family life.

Later Nimiipuu history describes councils and different leaders for fishing, hunting, war and religious responsibilities. This shows authority could be task-based and debated rather than a single throne. It is a specific nation's history, not a template to paste onto St'at'imc, Spokane, Ktunaxa or every earlier village.

Nimiipuu women carried technical, family and teaching knowledge, while mothers, fathers and other relatives helped children learn respectful conduct. A National Park Service account centers women whose expertise outsiders often minimized. It is later localized evidence and cannot assign every ancient basket, hearth or root tool to one gender.

At some Middle Fraser phases, differences in house size, storage or food access suggest inequality, yet households also defended autonomy and cooperated through networks. Archaeologists debate how durable leadership became. Unequal evidence deserves attention, but “complex hunter-gatherer” should never become a shortcut for kings, castes or one regional government.

The St'at'imc Nation continues governance and relationships with a homeland that includes rivers, mountains and seasonal resources. Citing that continuity prevents the atlas endpoint from becoming an extinction tale. It does not authorize using St'at'imc identity for all northern polygon points or for communities farther south.

sections.title: Let children learn through stories, observation, practice and play

items.text: Children learned by watching capable relatives, helping with age-appropriate work and hearing stories tied to conduct and place. A Nimiipuu education program asks who taught a child and how memory traveled through families. That is a later local comparison, not a recovered 500 BCE school timetable.

A stick game could practice attention, teamwork, rhythm and etiquette while remaining enjoyable. The surviving guide describes a Nimiipuu tradition, not a toy shared identically across the map. Games matter historically because skill and social rules can travel through laughter as effectively as through formal instruction.

Young people probably practiced gathering, fishing, tool care and route knowledge in steps, but archaeology seldom labels a learner's hand. A smaller point might be a practice piece, a finished tool or a broken fragment. Context, wear and manufacturing mistakes matter before an archaeologist calls something a child's object.

Living Plateau weaving joins plant knowledge, mathematics, touch, memory and design. Museum work with makers shows that baskets are not merely containers frozen behind glass. Children and apprentices can learn tension, spacing and repair from people. Ancient fragments should still be dated and localized before receiving a modern community name.

Language programs teach more than word lists: they connect pronunciation, relatives, humor, values and place. Yakama Ichishkiin and Spokane Salish programs demonstrate two distinct living traditions inside areas once covered by the broad color. Their difference is exactly why this card refuses to invent one Plateau language lesson.

sections.title: Study health, medicine, water and hygiene without guessing

items.text: Plants provided foods, fibers, woods and medicines in Nez Perce country, but a species can have several uses and charred remains do not name a remedy. A medicinal interpretation needs context or securely attributed knowledge. Living Nimiipuu plant teaching is evidence in its own right, not a prehistoric prescription book.

Long winters and stored food created practical health challenges: smoke, crowding, injuries, dental wear, spoiled supplies and fluctuating harvests. House floors and storage can test risk, but they do not diagnose individuals. Care may leave a healed injury or adapted workspace while the caregiver's name and treatment remain unknown.

Pipes and plant residues show that smoking in the inland Northwest has an archaeological history, sometimes involving tobacco and other plants. Chemical identification does not tell whether a particular use was medical, ceremonial or social. Context and community knowledge matter, and modern health effects should not be confused with ancient intention.

Clean water and waste separation are sensible needs, but the evidence does not support a shared sanitation system. Rivers could carry drinking water, fish and also contamination downstream. Camps likely used local routines for disposal and washing; without a securely identified facility, the honest toilet answer remains “not documented for this umbrella.”

Camas processing is also food safety. Slow cooking changes hard-to-digest carbohydrates, while expertise controls heat and time. The later stomachache story makes a funny warning, but archaeology must rely on ovens, bulbs and experiments. Knowledgeable preparation, rather than a magical plant property, made a dependable food.

sections.title: Approach ceremony, art, conflict and coercion with humility

items.text: More than ninety rock-art places have been recorded along the Columbia and tributaries, though dams submerged many. Images mark human choices and places, but their exact meanings cannot be read from shape alone. Descendant knowledge deserves authority, and archaeologists should resist turning every face or animal into a universal Plateau god.

An unusual structure at Keatley Creek has been interpreted as possible ritual architecture through its form, contents and relationship to nearby houses. “Possible” matters. Ceremonies can organize teaching and gathering, yet one building cannot prove a priesthood, temple system or shared religion across the polygon.

Competition, raiding and interpersonal violence occurred in some periods, while exchange, visiting and shared fisheries also required cooperation. Recent Plateau models link conflict partly to changing networks and autonomy. Archaeological trauma or defensive placement must be dated locally before becoming a story of constant warfare.

Coercion can hide behind attractive words such as “chief” or “trade.” Evidence for unequal storage or household size raises questions about obligation and access, but it does not automatically prove slavery, taxation or hereditary rule. Researchers compare several floors and households so one rich cache does not become an invented empire.

Syilx-led work to restore ntytyix, Chief Salmon, joins fisheries science, ceremony and responsibility after colonial dams disrupted runs. This is living continuity and repair, not a claim that present institutions are unchanged copies of 1500 BCE. It also shows why dammed rock art and fisheries are histories of power, not neutral modernization.

sections.title: Celebrate achievements while carrying history into the present

items.text: Managing camas for thousands of years without turning it into a domesticated crop is an achievement in observation, restraint and long planning. Harvesters selected mature bulbs, tended habitat and returned. That success challenges the idea that knowledge counts only when it produces farms, fences or a species redesigned by humans.

Kettle Falls drew repeated activity around a powerful fishery, and fifty radiocarbon dates reveal pulses rather than one unbroken crowd. Coordinating access, processing fish and maintaining relationships at such places was social technology. A famous fishing place could connect communities while they retained distinct languages and governments.

Schitsu'umsh and Ktunaxa official histories demonstrate living peoples with distinct names and languages inside portions of the old polygon. Ktunaxa is a language isolate, while Snchitsu'umshtsn belongs to a different history. Their coexistence turns linguistic diversity from a footnote into evidence against the atlas umbrella becoming one ethnicity.

The Nimiipuu, Yakama and Spokane nations continue governments, language programs and cultural work. Their endurance does not begin when the broad layer ends, and their histories do not need the typo-bearing label to validate them. The atlas can prompt questions, but living nations decide their own names, citizenship and teaching priorities.

In 1600 the atlas replaces this shrinking umbrella with many named Indigenous layers. The ending is continuity, not fall, conquest or extinction. Later horses, epidemics, missions, treaties, dams and settler states profoundly changed life, but they lie beyond this card's date and require nation-specific histories rather than one dramatic final sentence.

ending.text: The atlas ends the exact typo-bearing layer in 1600 after radically shrinking it in 1530. That endpoint is a redrawing seam, not a shared defeat, cultural fall or extinction. Distinct Nimiipuu, Yakama, Spokane, Schitsu'umsh, Ktunaxa, St'at'imc, Syilx and other peoples continue with their own governments, languages and homelands, so the override keeps fell null and invents no successor chain.
